Sunday, 9 June
Six months ago I made a list called 'Careers I'd like to steal': five people whose paths look like where I want to be in ten years. Two of them said yes to a monthly chat: Shreya, who went from testing to leading a platform team, and Mr Dsouza, who runs his own consultancy.
Today was my sixth chat with Shreya. I asked what actually mattered in her path. Not what I expected. She said the certification I'm studying for barely counted; what counted was volunteering, in year two, for the ugly migration project nobody wanted. Mr Dsouza said something similar last month about taking on client calls early.
So I'm changing the plan: dropping the second certification, and asking my lead for the next messy project instead.
Francis

subtype: Approach: rigid plan that ignores change [Pitfall]
passage:
Manager's note for Bhavna's file, March.
Two years ago I offered Bhavna a move to our new cloud data team. She said no, politely. 'It isn't in my five-year plan. I'm going deep in on-premise databases.' She showed me the plan, printed and laminated. I respected the discipline and didn't push.
Today we discussed the restructure. Most on-premise work moves to the cloud by next year, and her role is being merged. She was quiet for a long time, then said, 'I followed the plan exactly.' She did. The plan just didn't follow the world.
We agreed she will join the cloud team's training batch in April, and I've paired her with Ravi there. I told her the skills she has still count; she will just carry them somewhere new.
Ankita

qa.q: Which team did Ankita offer Bhavna two years ago?
qa.a: The new cloud data team.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she said 'I followed the plan exactly'?
qa.a: She was shaken and hurt, feeling that her discipline had been punished rather than rewarded.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do differently with her plan from now on?
qa.a: She could review it each year against where the field is heading, and treat a new opportunity as a reason to update the plan rather than refuse it.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel looking back at the refused offer?
qa.a: Ankita may feel some regret for not pushing harder, which may be why Bhavna is now paired with Ravi.

grounding: It shows a manager's note on an employee who treated a five-year plan as fixed, refused a growing area and later found the planned path shrinking.

Bhupen got the lead role on the AI tools team today. Two years ago the same offer came to me first. I said no because my plan, the one on my wall, said 'Year 3: senior mobile developer'. Mobile was the map. AI was off the map.
Today my manager told me the mobile team is shrinking to four people next year. I stood in the parking lot feeling stupid, holding a coffee I didn't drink.

Tomorrow I'm taking the plan off the wall. Not throwing it away. Just writing on top of it, in pencil: 'Review every six months. Anything new gets a real look.'

Coaching note, session 3.
Disha arrived with her five-year plan, which last month had been only job titles. Today it had a second column she called 'Life'. In it: marriage, probably in two years; her parents in Indore, her father's knees getting worse; and her own back pain from long sitting, which her doctor had asked her to take seriously.
She had then set limits beside each career goal. The promotion to team lead stays, but not through constant weekend work: one weekend a month at most. A trip to Indore every quarter goes into the calendar before project deadlines do. A walk every lunch break.
She said, 'Last year my career plan ate everything else.' I've asked her to try the limits for three months and bring back what held and what broke.
Suraj

qa.a: 'Life'.

Missed Nandini's cousin's engagement on Sunday for a release. Third family event this year. Amma called tonight and didn't complain, which was worse.
So I sat down with my career plan and did what I should have done in January: wrote down what else matters. Nandini and I want to marry next winter. Amma and Appa are both over sixty-five. My sleep is a mess, and I haven't played badminton in eight months.
New rules, next to the career goals: no work on Sundays except real incidents. Leave on time on Wednesdays for badminton. Two trips home a year, booked in January like any deadline.

In a glass meeting room in Barcelona, Pablo stood at the whiteboard with three coloured markers. The launch date fight had been going on for two weeks. Soo-ah, the lead engineer, watched him draw three circles: Sales, Engineering, Finance.
Under each he wrote two lines. The first was what they kept saying. Sales: 'Launch in March.' Engineering: 'We need two more months.' Finance: 'No extra spending.' The second line was what they actually cared about. Sales: a big client's contract renews in April. Engineering: last year's rushed launch caused a month of night-time fixes. Finance: the budget review in May.
Soo-ah leaned forward. 'So Sales needs that one client happy by April, not the whole product.'
'Exactly,' Pablo said, and circled it.

qa.a: In April.

qa.a: It suggests Soo-ah felt interested and hopeful, seeing a way through the fight once the real concerns were written down.

In the hospital's small IT room, Lalit had a new patient-registration system to deliver and three groups pulling at him. Himani from the finance office had come down to argue about cost again.
Instead of arguing, Lalit pulled a sheet of chart paper across the table. 'Let me draw who's in this.' Doctors, front-desk nurses, IT, finance. For each, he wrote what they had demanded in emails, then asked Himani to help him write what they really needed.
Front desk: 'a faster system' really meant shorter queues at 9 a.m. IT: 'more testing' really meant not losing patient records. Finance, Himani said, 'less money' really meant staying inside this year's grant.
Looking at the sheet, Lalit saw that the 9 a.m. queue could be eased with one extra registration screen, without touching the grant.

'Everyone has the one-page brief?' Jyoti asked. Eight heads nodded. 'Three options for the warehouse system: fix the old one, buy the vendor product, or build our own. Costs and risks are on the page. Each team gets five minutes. Maria, operations first.'
Maria stood. 'Building our own takes eighteen months. We can't wait that long; our pickers are losing an hour a day now.'
'Noted. Finance?'
'The vendor option is cheapest over five years, if the licence price holds.'
'IT?'
'The vendor product doesn't talk to our billing system without extra work.'
After forty minutes, Jyoti wrote on the board: 'Decision: vendor product, with a budget for billing integration. Reasons: fastest relief for operations, lowest five-year cost.' She read it aloud. 'This goes in the minutes today. Anyone who disagrees, tell me why by Friday.'
Maria sat back. 'At least we all got heard.'

qa.q: How long would building their own system take?
qa.a: Eighteen months.

qa.q: How does Maria seem to feel at the end?
qa.a: Maria seems satisfied, even relieved, that every team got heard, whatever the outcome.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti do to make the decision stick?
qa.a: She could share the minutes with the reasons, answer any Friday objections openly and review the choice after the first few months.

qa.q: How might the IT team see the decision?
qa.a: IT's concern about billing was heard and given a budget, so they may accept the choice even though it adds work.

grounding: It shows a lead circulating a one-page brief of options, costs and risks, giving each group five minutes and recording the decision and reasons.

I'm Trisha, and last month I ran my first decision meeting that didn't end in shouting. We had to choose a city for the new support centre: Jaipur, Kochi or Indore. Before, these meetings were a free-for-all. This time I sent a one-page brief two days early: three options, costs, hiring risks, travel time. In the meeting, each department got exactly five minutes, timer on the table. I said nothing except 'thank you, next'.
Nilesh from HR argued hard for Kochi. When the group chose Indore, I wrote the reasons on the board: lower rents, faster hiring, one direct flight. I emailed the notes within an hour.
Nilesh stopped me in the corridor later. 'I still think Kochi was better,' he said. 'But I get why. It felt fair.' That was the part I wanted.

qa.q: How long did each department get to speak?
qa.a: Exactly five minutes, with a timer on the table.

qa.q: How does Trisha feel about Nilesh's comment in the corridor?
qa.a: Trisha feels satisfied and proud, because fairness was exactly what the meeting was meant to achieve.

qa.q: What else could Trisha add to make future decisions even fairer?
qa.a: Trisha could invite written comments after the notes go out and state when the decision will be reviewed.

qa.q: How did the meeting look to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh still preferred Kochi, but seeing the reasons written down after everyone was heard made the process feel fair to him.

grounding: It shows a lead sending a one-page brief with options, costs and risks, giving each group five minutes and recording the decision and reasons.
